title: Elizabeth Fry
hook: a Quaker woman walks into the women's side of Newgate prison, sits down, and reads

segments.voice: Yesterday, Newman on a windless sea, asking to be led and not to see the distant scene. Your line was one step enough. What was the step you took? Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

The door to the women's side of Newgate prison in London opens, and a woman in plain Quaker clothes steps through. Inside: women awaiting trial and women already sentenced, crowded together, some with their children, short of clothes and short of hope. The story told about that first visit is that the keepers warned her it wasn't safe, and that she went in anyway. She doesn't preach at anyone. She sits down. She asks about the children. Later she reads aloud from the Bible. Her name is Elizabeth Fry, a wife, a mother, and a Quaker minister. Today, what one woman did by sitting down in the wrong room.

Start with where she came from. Fry was a Quaker, a member of the Religious Society of Friends. Their founder, George Fox, told his followers to "walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one." Every one. That includes the woman in the next cell and the woman who stole bread. Fry took it literally. Now, what she actually did. She didn't start with a speech about reform. She started a small school inside the prison for the children who were living there with their mothers. She brought in sewing and knitting so the women could work and earn something. She gathered a group of women visitors to come back week after week. And by the usual account, she asked the prisoners themselves to agree to the rules of the new arrangement, instead of handing rules down. Then she read. Plainly, out loud, from the Bible. Which passage sat behind all of it? A scene in Matthew where the king says to the righteous, in the King James Bible, "I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me." The righteous ask when they ever did that, and he answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." To Fry, a prison visit was not charity from above. It was meeting Christ in a cell. Her work spread beyond Newgate. She visited women on ships carrying convicts overseas, and she spoke to members of Parliament about how prisons were run. Churches still send visitors into prisons today. The work still begins the same way: someone walks in and sits down.
screen: `I WAS IN PRISON, AND YE CAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write to a prisoner. Settle, and breathe. If you know someone who is inside, bring their face to mind and write them a few honest lines: what your week was like, and that you thought of them. If you don't know anyone, write a short note to a stranger in prison, someone you'll never meet. Keep it plain. No advice, no lecture. Just: you're a person, and someone remembered you today. Some churches and charities run letter programs, if you decide later to send it. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. The bell holds the time.
Elizabeth Fry. A Quaker minister who walked into Newgate, sat with the women and their children, and helped change how prisons treated them.
Your line: I was in prison. Today, notice one person the world has locked out, in a cell or just in a corner, and go toward them instead of away. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: In some churches, prison ministry teams visit people in jail, lead Bible studies, write letters and support families, often pointing to Matthew 25 as the reason.
